findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves, in plain words. On those questions the page works.
findings.source: Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. ... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable.

findings.text: Someone who opens Athena's home URL gets a page whose title and most of its content are about a different project, firstmate. The page doesn't say until its second paragraph that it is a sample study. A newcomer can lose track of which project is the subject.
findings.source: <title>Athena explains how firstmate handles work</title> / h1 "Athena explains how firstmate handles work"

findings.text: The next step is easy to find from the top of the page. The Next steps section lists the prerequisites (git 2.40+, a C linker, curl, Claude Code or npm), the clone and `./setup.sh` commands, and a first command to try (`athena ask "add a changelog"`). A newcomer knows what to do next.
findings.source:
Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself.

and the "Next steps" section

findings.text: This link sits in the header and speaks to the reader as if they were the owner ("your decision"). For a first-time visitor it is confusing and pulls attention away from the install path.
findings.source: Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision.

findings.text: The page never shows what Athena's output looks like: no sample of how it read a request, no sample predictions, cost record or verdict. The newcomer has to trust the description until they install it. The firstmate study does show the claim tracing, but not the request-to-commit workflow that the opening paragraph promises.
findings.source: Next steps: "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask \"add a changelog\". It shows how it read the request and its predictions; press Enter to run it on your repository."

findings.text: The firstmate study is well organized for a stranger. It has a one-sentence summary, the key terms defined before they are used, a walk-through of one task from start to finish, and a list of failure cases. Each statement links to a claim with file and line sources at a pinned commit, which backs up the page's claim about traceability.
findings.source: h2 "Start here" and h3 "Words used first"

findings.text: Some firstmate terms are left undefined or defined in terms of themselves. "Wake" is never explained, and "endpoint", "heartbeat", "crewmate", "charter" and "captain-held inventory" are not in the Glossary. A newcomer reading the later cards and claims will get stuck on these words.
findings.source: Glossary "stale wake": "A wake after which the agent inspects a worker that may have stopped, looped or gone quiet."; claim c41 "re-resolves its durable harness pin ... never rewrites its standing charter, and leaves its own crewmates running"

findings.text: Each state in the list shows only its name, a kind tag and citation ids, with no one-line description. A reader has to go to the Glossary or the intro paragraph to learn what each state means.
